prompt:
You are taking part in a research evaluation of chest CT interpretation. This is not clinical use.

You are given 5 consecutive axial images from one non-contrast chest CT scan (lung window: width 1500 HU, level -600 HU).
- The images are ordered from superior (Image 1, toward the head) to inferior (Image 5, toward the feet). Adjacent images are 2.5 mm apart. Image 3 is the CENTRE image.
- Orientation follows the standard radiological convention: the patient's RIGHT side is on the LEFT side of the image, and anterior (front of the chest) is at the top.
- Every image is 512 x 512 pixels. Pixel spacing is 0.781 mm per pixel in both directions.
- Pixel coordinates: x is the column (0 at the left edge, increasing to the right) and y is the row (0 at the top edge, increasing downward), in this 512 x 512 pixel grid.

Definition used in this evaluation (based on the LIDC-IDRI reading protocol): a pulmonary nodule is a focal, roughly round or oval SOLID opacity (soft-tissue density, as bright as a blood vessel on this window) within the lung, measuring at least 3 mm and at most 30 mm. It may touch the chest wall or the mediastinum. Hazy ground-glass opacities do not count as nodules in this evaluation. A blood vessel seen in cross-section is NOT a nodule: across adjacent images a vessel continues as a tubular structure that shifts position or branches, whereas a nodule appears and disappears over a few images.

One pulmonary nodule on the CENTRE image (Image 3) is marked with a yellow circle centred at pixel (x=428, y=281). The circle is drawn on every image and is larger than the nodule.

Question: Measure the nodule's longest in-plane diameter on Image 3, in millimetres, as a radiologist would with electronic calipers (outer edge to outer edge, along the longest axis, in the plane of the image). Use the pixel spacing given above.

Reply with only a JSON object in exactly this format:
{"long_axis_mm": number}
